title: Machine learning prioritizes ruthenium complexes with increased MRSA antibacterial hit rates
summary: Researchers trained machine-learning models on 288 modularly synthesized ruthenium arene Schiff-base complexes and used them to prioritize 54 new compounds for antibacterial-activity testing. The model-selected set had a 53.7% hit rate against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, compared with 9.4% in the original library, an approximately 5.7-fold enrichment.
ai_technology: Machine-learning activity-prediction models trained on ruthenium arene Schiff-base complex structures and antibacterial assay data
organization: University of Bern Department of Chemistry, Biochemistry & Pharmaceutical Sciences; National University of Singapore Department of Chemistry

evidence.tested: Researchers trained machine-learning models on 288 modularly synthesized ruthenium arene Schiff-base complexes and used them to prioritize 54 new compounds for antibacterial-activity testing.
evidence.unknown: This is a study-specific in-vitro antibacterial hit-rate enrichment, not animal efficacy, clinical validation, or an approved antibiotic. The comparison is 54 model-selected compounds vs the 288-complex source library, not a randomized prospective comparison with all possible metal complexes.
evidence.ai_role: Models were trained using assay data from 288 modularly synthesized ruthenium complexes and used to predict activity for a new set of 54 compounds. Those prioritized compounds were then assessed for antibacterial activity; the paper reports higher MRSA hit-rate in the model-selected set than in the original library.
